title: How the Moon was made
text: A planet the size of Mars hits the young Earth, and the wreckage becomes the Moon — as the computer models tell it. 4,567 million years ago. Around the young Sun, dust sticks into pebbles, pebbles into rocks, and rocks into small planets. The Earth grows by swallowing them. Each crash heats it, and much of its surface may be molten rock. Then a planet about the size of Mars — scientists call it Theia — hits the Earth a glancing blow. Molten rock and hot vapour are thrown into space, and form a glowing ring around the Earth. In the computer models the ring clumps together into one Moon very fast — in years, or perhaps a few centuries. The new Moon is many times closer than today. Its pull raises tides that slow the Earth’s spin and push the Moon away. It is still moving away: about 3.8 cm a year, measured with lasers bounced off mirrors the Apollo astronauts left. The Earth cools. By about 4.4 billion years ago it has a hard crust, and liquid water.
prompt:
A painting for a natural-history museum: How the Moon was made, about 4567 million years ago.
Painted in the manner of Charles R. Knight (1874–1953), the American natural-history muralist: oil on canvas, confident visible brushwork, warm golden naturalistic light, soft atmospheric haze, a palette of ochres, siennas, olive greens and dusty blues, calm and dignified realism. Keep his warmth and his eye for the real world, but follow TODAY's science, not the science of his time: paint the land, water, plants and climate exactly as described here.
What happened, from the scientific evidence: A planet the size of Mars hits the young Earth, and the wreckage becomes the Moon — as the computer models tell it. 4,567 million years ago. Around the young Sun, dust sticks into pebbles, pebbles into rocks, and rocks into small planets. The Earth grows by swallowing them. Each crash heats it, and much of its surface may be molten rock. Then a planet about the size of Mars — scientists call it Theia — hits the Earth a glancing blow. Molten rock and hot vapour are thrown into space, and form a glowing ring around the Earth. In the computer models the ring clumps together into one Moon very fast — in years, or perhaps a few centuries. The new Moon is many times closer than today. Its pull raises tides that slow the Earth’s spin and push the Moon away. It is still moving away: about 3.8 cm a year, measured with lasers bounced off mirrors the Apollo astronauts left. The Earth cools. By about 4.4 billion years ago it has a hard crust, and liquid water.
Paint the moment as seen from high in the sky: a wide view of the land and sea where it happened, as they were THEN — the continents, coasts, plants and life of that time, not today's. Show only what the description says. Living things only where it names them, small, as they are reconstructed today; none where it does not.
No text, labels, map lines, arrows, borders or frame.
differs: No one knows what the body that hit the Earth looked like; the sizes and the look of the two worlds are the painter's guess.
